newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans gingerly test offshore investment waters.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans gingerly test offshore investment waters.

text.p: South Africans were forbidden to invest any money outside the country for over 30 years.
Now the rules have been relaxed, but most people with savings to salt away offshore have been very cautious in testing the waters.

Institutions and investment advisers say they have received plenty of interest in their new investment products, but very little business has been done since the exchange control regulations were eased on Tuesday.
"We are seeing a fair amount of interest... there are a lot of enquiries," said Stephen Grundling, national sales manager at Templeton Asset Management.
"But people are tending to be cautious and are not leaping in."

On Tuesday, South African residents were allowed to invest up to 200,000 rand ($44,250) in offshore assets for the first time since 1961, when the country took independence from Britain and left the Commonwealth and introduced exchange controls.
The latest step, part of the government's phased removal of the tight controls, has generated a welter of advertisements from competing institutions.
But it has also resulted in words of caution from the authorities, which analysts say has left people confused.

"It's new products, a new concept ...there are a lot of warnings in the press that investors should be aware about where they should invest, what they should invest in and the tax implications," said Charl le Roux, managing director of Sanlam Unit Trusts.
"People are still evaluating and seeing what's out there," Grundling said. "They are more confused than anything else."
He added that the business of investing offshore should pick up over the next month or so.

The financial markets have taken heart from the slow pace of offshore investment. The rand has firmed two cents against the dollar since Tuesday as institutions which had accumulated dollars, anticipating increased demand, sold them back into the market. Bond yields posted 17-month lows later in the week.

Charles Jonker, head of financial economics and strategy at Absa Bank, said that once demand did pick up, however, there was unlikely to be a rush of capital from the country which had been feared by some.
The Reserve Bank has estimated that between three and five billion rand could leave the country, while some economists have predicted amounts of up to 15 billion leaving the country.
Jonker noted, however, that of those who could afford to take 200,000 rand offshore, most of them were highly indebted.
He said a study done by Absa bank showed that individuals who earned around 200,000 rand were high up on the credit facility list.
"Furthermore, if one looks at the savings rate in South Africa there is no savings from the personal side. There is only contractual savings," he said.

As a result, he said he expected most demand to centre on unit trusts bought by monthly subscription rather than lump sum payments. This was borne out by the fact that most overseas investment products on offer were linked to unit trusts.
Economists estimate there are around 100,000 "high-net-worth individuals" in South Africa -- the kind of people who would be expected to have some money to invest outside the country's borders.

Jonker added that he also expected the flood of portfolio investment into South Africa to double from current levels by year-end -- more than compensating for an outflow of three to five billion rand.
